blocks.p: The rain on Daphne fell at the second hour after noon, and Sol learned to read by it.

It came out of a clear sky, fine and soft and perfectly straight, because the processors on the ridge released it then, and in three weeks it had never once been late. It was the only thing on Daphne anyone trusted. Everything else could die. The whole world was green, a green so bright it looked wet even when it was dry, but it was a single layer thick: moss and short grass laid over grey rock like a cloth over a table. The settlers walked on boardwalks, because a boot print in the moss stayed brown for a year. They grew their orchards under white nets on terraces held up by dry-stone walls that slid a little every spring, and where the walls had failed, the rock showed through the green like bone through a thin cheek.

Sol lodged in the loft of the seed house at Long Terrace, and every afternoon he opened the loft door on the rain and sat in it with Stephen’s grey notebook on his knees. The original stayed wrapped at the bottom of his case; a whole leaf of it had come away in his hand on the crossing, and he had not dared since. The copy would do. It was Stephen’s hand, small and slanting and pressed hard, running to every edge of every page.

He had begun at the first page, the way a man reads any book, and it had taken him most of a month to come through the old law and the kings and the prophets. It was the Book of Life, and it was not. He recognized it, and he did not. The rooms were in the same order, and there were whole wings he had lived beside all his life without knowing they were there. In the Book of Life every story ran uphill into Life. In this one people died, and were mourned, and the mourning was written down as though it mattered. And Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.

And nothing took it from him in the night. In the cell on Serenity, Stephen had said a name to him twice, and twice it had slid away like a word on waking. Now what he read was still there in the morning, like a coat left on a chair. His head was his own.
In the songs, in his second week, he found the city.

Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God. His holy mountain, beautiful in its height, is the joy of all the earth: Mount Zion. Stephen had spelled it the old way, with a Z, and in the margin, very small, he had written: Sion. Yes. That one. Sol read the line four times. He had said the name every day of his remembered life. He had stood in the Holy City eleven times and never once asked what it was called for; it was the Holy City, and the name was the name, the way Life was Life. And here it was, a hill. A real one, of stone, in a small hot country, with a wall round it and a king who wrote songs on it. A hill a man could walk up in an hour. Someone had lifted its name off it and set it over a city of glass, and he had never thought to wonder where the word had come from.
In his third week on Daphne he came past the last of the prophets to a new beginning. The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
He stopped with his finger under the first name.

He knew it before he had finished reading it. It was the name Stephen had said in the white cell, the second one that belonged with the first, the one he had heard and lost. He looked out at the rain and counted to ten and looked back. It was still there. He said it aloud, to no one, with the rain falling a hand’s breadth from his knees.
“Jesus.”
It stayed.

Then the list: fathers and sons, each one born and each one gone. It seemed to Sol that he was walking down a long corridor of the dead, and that the book was taking the trouble to remember each of them, and that at the end of the corridor a child was born and laid in a manger.

He had to ask Hesper Dunne, who kept the seed house, what a manger was. A feed trough, she said, for the goats. He had haloed tens of thousands of infants. He had sung over cradles of white linen under the gold of the great Windows and laid two fingers on soft temples and given every child the coin under the skin that would keep it forever. No sacrament had been said over this one. Nothing had been set under his skin to keep him.
Sol read the four accounts in twelve days. He could not read them quickly.

He had expected a doctrine. He had stood before God eleven times, before a face that wanted nothing from him and gave him everything, and he had expected something like that. What he found was a man who got tired. He sat down by a well at noon and asked a woman for a drink. He fell asleep in a boat in a storm. He went to dinners and was criticized for the company he kept. When a blind man was brought to him, he did not wait to be asked for something. He asked. What do you want me to do for you? Sol, who had heard a lifetime of petitions at the Windows, laid the notebook face down on his knee and sat a long time with the rain.
A man full of leprosy came to him and knelt and begged him, “If you are willing, you can make me clean.” Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him.

He remembered his own hand flat on the tiles of the Bounty Market, a hand’s breadth from the old man’s head. Not touching him. He had been proud of that, he realized. He had thought it was compassion.
Then the boy. Teacher, I brought my son to you. Wherever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. It has often thrown him into fire and into water.

Sol read it three times, with the skin tightening along his arms. He knew it as he knew his own hand. He had knelt beside it in a market. He had watched it take Teo Thorne and seen his sister’s face above him. He had felt it from the inside. The crowd stood around the boy on the ground until he lay still, like a corpse, so that most of them said, “He is dead.” But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.
No warden had come in white. No one had covered a child’s ears. He had taken the boy by the hand.

The father’s cry was in the same passage, and it was in Sol’s mouth before he had finished reading it. I believe; help my unbelief. He said it many times in those twelve days. He did not know a truer prayer.

He found himself in the book too, and never where he would have wished. He was in the crowd that said he is dead. He was in the council room on the night they decided, where the most reasonable man present said, kindly, that it is better for you that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation should perish. Sol knew that voice. He had used it at his own desk, signing for the infected, for their sake and for everyone’s peace. It was a gentle voice. It sounded like mercy.
Then they killed him.

Stephen had told him, because he did, and still he was not ready. He read it in all four, as if four men who had stood in different places were trying to tell him exactly what they had seen. The whipping. The thorns. They took him out through the gate of the city whose hill he had found in the songs, to another hill, close enough to walk to, and the book gave its name too: the place called the Skull. The Holy City had been named for the first hill. No one had ever told him about the second. The nails, which the book did not describe, because everyone who first read it had known what nails did. And in the third account a line that stopped his breath, because he had heard it before.
Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.

He heard Stephen say it in the white room under the ice, with the wardens’ calm hands on him, looking past Sol at someone Sol could not see. Do not hold this against him. Stephen had not made it up. He had learned it here, from this man, and carried it all the way to Serenity and given it to the one who had signed for him. They do not know what they are doing. Sol had not known. That was the only mercy in it, and it was not his own.

He breathed his last, the book said. Sol closed it and went out along the boardwalk without a coat, to the end of the terrace where the wall had failed, and stood on the bare grey rock in the rain until the fourth hour, when it stopped exactly on time.
He read the end the next day.

A woman went to the grave in the dark and found it open, and stood outside it weeping. Not one line of the Book of Life was spoken to a weeping woman. In this book angels spoke to her, and then a man she took for the gardener, and they all asked her the same thing. Woman, why are you weeping? Not stop. Not forget. Why.
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Teacher.”
Sol put his hand over his mouth.

He knew how that felt: to be called by your name where you had expected no one to know it, by a voice that spoke it as though you were friends. It had happened to him once, on the floor of a market, and broken him open. Stephen had only been doing what had first been done for him.
Tobin came up the ladder at lamp-lighting with his kit bag over one shoulder and found Sol sitting on the floor against the seed sacks with the closed notebook in his lap.
“You’ve got to the end,” Tobin said.
“Of the four.”
Tobin lowered himself onto an upturned crate and looked at Sol for a while in the lamplight. Then he said, without any particular weight, “You’re going grey. Did you know?”
Sol did not. He turned to the dark glass of the loft window, and a man looked back at him with a streak of white at each temple, as if something had been spilled there and dried.

“Two months and more,” Tobin said. “That’s about right. It went the same with Stephen, only he was older to start with.” He unbuckled the bag. “He gave me something to keep for you. Said when you’d read the four, not before. Said otherwise you’d argue with him instead of with the book.”
It was a maintenance ledger of the kind the relay stations used, its brown cover cracked across and mended with tape.
“He said if it went the way he thought, sooner or later you’d come to me,” Tobin said. “I told him that was the stupidest thing I’d ever heard. He said yes, probably.”
The entries were dated by renewals, not by days, and all of them began the same way.

Dear Stephen, you won’t believe this, so I’ll be quick. There’s a book in your bag. Your mother gave it to you. You had a mother; she sang badly and meant it. If you’re reading this with a smooth face and no idea who wrote it, they’ve been at you again. Don’t panic. Read the book. Start with the fourth account. You always liked a good first line.

Sol read through the night. It was all there, in pieces, the way Stephen had got it back. Dear Stephen, today I remembered the speech. The big one, the first year, in the stadium with half the seats burned. “A human hand on the controls. Never again.” I was very good. They cried, which they still could then, and I told them they’d never have to again. Of everything, that’s the line I’d take back. And in a hand that shook: Renewal in six days. I’ll go just once more. That’s how a man stays away from home for four hundred years.

Near the middle was an entry Sol could not read twice. Dear Stephen, I remembered Sol today. You’ll want to know who that is. He was the best man you ever knew and he didn’t believe a word of it. He peeled oranges in one piece. You prayed for him every night for twenty years and he never knew. Start again.
The last page was not addressed to Stephen.

Dear Sol. You always read the ending first, so I’ve put this at the back. There’s no future Stephen; I’m going to Mars in the morning. I don’t know how it goes after that, but I know how it ends, and so do you now, so don’t let anyone tell you it ends there. Be kind to Tobin. He thinks he isn’t clever. He’s the cleverest of us; he never needed a book to know whose he was. Hello, Sol. It’s good to see you.
For once in his life, Sol thought, he had not read the ending first. He sat with that until the lamp burned down.
The church at Long Terrace began with grief, because on Daphne there was a great deal of it.

The renewal suite at Daphne Landing had been failing for a year, and the ascension relay dropped one soul in three. A circuit priest came three times a year to say the Remembrance, and between his visits people fell from the terraces and took fevers and were caught under the walls when they slid. Their families were told not to mourn, and on Daphne a good many of them could not manage it.

Mattie Kerr had gone into the water a year before, at Tobin’s hands, on a dock at Plenty, and had written to him since that some of her neighbors were asking things she could not answer. Hesper Dunne was the first of them. Her husband had been under the slide on the fourth terrace in the spring, and his ascension had come back Not received, and she had been told to be calm. Five months later she was still shaking, and Mattie had sat with her among his seed sacks and said a name.

They met in the seed house after dark, by one lamp. Six came the first night, and then more than the room would hold, so that they sat on the ladder and stood in the door. Sol read to them from Stephen’s copy. He had read aloud all his life, in cathedrals, to thousands who knew every word before he said it. He had never read to people who interrupted. They asked what a shepherd was. A wall builder named Abel Strand, who had come to argue, asked whether the man in the book had truly wept at his friend’s grave, knowing he was about to raise him. Sol said yes. Abel asked why. Sol said he did not know. Abel looked at him for a long moment, and came back the next night without his arguments.

In the fifth week Sol baptized Hesper Dunne in the cold outflow below the processors, standing in it to his waist. He had laid two fingers on more temples than he could count, and he had never once held anyone’s head. Her hair was coarse and wet, and her neck was rigid with fear.
“Does it hurt?” she whispered.
“It’s cold,” he said.

She went under, and came up gasping, and put her fingers to her temple, and he watched her face change. He knew that look from the inside: a woman listening to a silence she had never heard before, and finding that she was not alone in it.
He baptized eleven that night while Tobin held the lamp on the bank. Eleven Halos dark. Eleven fewer threads running up the line to whatever fed at the other end.

The valley noticed. And because the word they had heard through the seed house walls was a word no one was allowed to say, they said it the way children say forbidden words, low and quick, half delighted and half afraid, and they made something out of it to throw.
Sol heard it first from a boy of perhaps ten who ran past the seed house door at dusk, shouted it in at them, and ran on into the dark, shrieking at his own daring.
“Christians!”
Hesper went white. “If the circuit priest hears that...”
“He’ll hear it,” Tobin said.

Sol was listening to the word, which seemed to hang in the doorway after the boy had gone. It had been built out of the name, and meant as an insult. It was the first new word he had heard in longer than he could remember, and it was not new at all. It had the feel of a word that had been waiting a long time to be said again.
“Let them,” he said.
The next evening a woman from the lower terrace stood in the door with her hands twisted in her apron and asked whether this was where the Christians met. Mattie Kerr told her it was.
It came for him three nights later, while he was reading to them about the woman at the grave.

He felt the thumb behind his left eye and knew it now; Lucan had given it a name and taught him what to do. “Tobin,” he said, and shut the notebook and held it out, and felt Tobin’s hand close on it, and the lamp went very bright, and...
...and it was raining.

Not Daphne’s rain. This came sideways and cold, whenever it liked, and it smelled of hot stone and of something black and oily that had baked in the sun all day and was giving its heat back up into the wet. His shoes were full of water. He stood on soaked grass among a crowd of people under black umbrellas, and he was holding one, the curved handle cold in his fist, tilting it toward someone beside him. In front of them the ground was open, a long raw cut in the earth that smelled of iron and roots. A woman near the front was singing. She was off the note, badly off, and she did not stop, and he could hear in her voice that she meant every word. The rain ran down his face and into his collar, and he could not tell whether it was only rain.
He came back on the floor of the seed house.

There was a ceiling of rough boards and a smell of hay, and his tongue was thick and tasted of copper, and every muscle he owned ached as if he had been carrying stone. Someone had folded a shawl under his head. He thought for a moment, stupidly, that it was his own robe.

No one had run. That was the first thing he understood, slowly, the way everything came slowly afterward. The room was still full. They had pulled back to give him space and sat in a ring, watching him, and not one of them had covered anyone’s ears. Mattie’s daughter Wren, nine years old, sat cross-legged beside his head holding his hand in both of hers. Tobin knelt at his other side with the notebook buttoned safe inside his jacket.
“Two minutes,” Tobin said. “Bit less.”
“You talked,” Wren said. “After. We listened.”
Sol tried to ask her what he had said. What came out instead, thick and slow, was, “Where’s the umbrella?”
Wren looked at Tobin. Tobin looked at Sol.
“What’s an umbrella?” Wren said.

He did not know. He reached for it and found only the cold curved handle in his fist, and the rain drumming on the black cloth, and the singing that would not stop. And that he had been holding it out over someone beside him to keep them dry, while the rain ran down into his own collar.
He lay on the floor of the seed house with a child’s hand in his, and tried, and could not see who.
